**Conventions.** For a continuous $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb C$ and $a\le p\le q\le b$, write $f=u+iv$ with $u=\operatorname{Re}f$, $v=\operatorname{Im}f$ real-valued, and define
$$\int_p^q f(t)\,dt := \int_p^q u(t)\,dt + i\int_p^q v(t)\,dt,$$
the right-hand integrals being real Riemann integrals; as usual $\int_p^p g = 0$. Since $|u(s)-u(t)|\le|f(s)-f(t)|$ and likewise for $v$, $u$ and $v$ are continuous on $[a,b]$, hence on every closed subinterval $[p,q]$; continuous real functions on compact intervals are Riemann integrable, so all integrals below exist.

**Lemma.** Let $g:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and $c\in[a,b]$. Then $\int_a^c g+\int_c^b g=\int_a^b g$.

*Proof.* If $c=a$ the left side is $0+\int_a^b g$; if $c=b$ it is $\int_a^b g+0$. So assume $a<c<b$. For a partition $P$ of an interval write $L(g,P)$, $U(g,P)$ for the lower and upper Darboux sums; for integrable $g$ the integral equals $\sup_P L(g,P)=\inf_P U(g,P)$, and refining a partition does not decrease lower sums nor increase upper sums.

Let $P$ be any partition of $[a,b]$ and $P^*=P\cup\{c\}$. Then $P^*$ splits as $P_1=P^*\cap[a,c]$, a partition of $[a,c]$, and $P_2=P^*\cap[c,b]$, a partition of $[c,b]$, and the subintervals of $P^*$ are exactly those of $P_1$ together with those of $P_2$. Hence
$$L(g,P)\le L(g,P^*)=L(g,P_1)+L(g,P_2)\le \int_a^c g+\int_c^b g,$$
$$U(g,P)\ge U(g,P^*)=U(g,P_1)+U(g,P_2)\ge \int_a^c g+\int_c^b g.$$
Taking the supremum over $P$ in the first line gives $\int_a^b g\le \int_a^c g+\int_c^b g$, and the infimum in the second gives $\int_a^b g\ge \int_a^c g+\int_c^b g$. $\blacksquare$

**Theorem.** $\int_a^c f+\int_c^b f=\int_a^b f$.

*Proof.* Applying the Lemma to $u$ and to $v$ (both continuous on $[a,b]$),
$$\int_a^c f+\int_c^b f=\Big(\int_a^c u+i\int_a^c v\Big)+\Big(\int_c^b u+i\int_c^b v\Big)
=\Big(\int_a^c u+\int_c^b u\Big)+i\Big(\int_a^c v+\int_c^b v\Big)=\int_a^b u+i\int_a^b v=\int_a^b f.$$
$\blacksquare$
